title: Americans Still Need $110,000 to Afford the Typical Home as Affordability Barely Budges
excerpt: A new Redfin report finds the income required to buy the median U.S. home has stayed near record highs, leaving the typical household $22,000 short.
body:
• A household needs $109,796 per year to afford the median-priced U.S. home, just 0.5% below last year's record high of $110,382, according to Redfin.
  • The typical American household earns $87,599 — roughly $22,200 less than what's needed to comfortably buy a home.
  • Only three major metros (St. Louis, Indianapolis, and Pittsburgh) have median incomes that exceed what's needed to afford the local typical home.
  • Seattle, San Jose, and Portland saw the largest affordability improvements, while San Francisco remains the least affordable metro at $453,205 needed.

Americans need to earn nearly $110,000 a year to comfortably afford the typical home for sale, and that figure has barely moved in the past 12 months despite modest improvements in the housing market, according to a new Redfin report.

The Numbers

A household would need an annual income of $109,796 to purchase the median-priced U.S. home in June 2026 while spending no more than 30% of income on housing costs, Redfin found. That is just 0.5% below the record high of $110,382 a year ago, according to USA Today's analysis of the report.

The median U.S. household earned an estimated $87,599 in June, up 4% from a year ago. The median home sale price rose 2.2% over the same period. Mortgage rates eased slightly but remained in the mid-6% range, keeping borrowing costs elevated.

"The earnings needed to buy a house have stabilized after several years of deterioration, but that doesn't mean homes are affordable to the average American."

— Yingqi Xu, Senior Economist, Redfin

The Gap Is Narrowing, Slowly

The income gap — the difference between what Americans earn and what they need to afford a home — has shrunk from $28,900 two years ago to $26,100 last year to $22,200 now. That improvement is driven almost entirely by rising incomes rather than falling home prices, according to Redfin.

The typical homebuyer would need to spend 37.6% of income on a median-priced home, down from 39.3% last year. Meanwhile, 34.2% of homes for sale were affordable for households earning the national median income in June, up from 30.5% a year earlier. But affordability remains well below pre-2022 levels, when more than half of listings were within reach of the typical household.

Where Affordability Is Improving — and Where It Isn't

Affordability improved in 24 of the 46 major metro areas Redfin analyzed. Seattle led the pack, with the income needed to afford the typical home falling 7.4% as home prices declined. San Jose saw a 6.5% drop, and Portland followed at 4.5%.

At the other extreme, San Francisco remained the nation's least affordable major metro. Buyers there need an annual income of $453,205 to afford the typical home. Only three major metros — St. Louis, Indianapolis, and Pittsburgh — had median household incomes that exceeded what's needed to buy locally.

What This Means for Indian Americans

Indian American households earn a median income well above the national figure, with Census data consistently placing them among the highest-earning demographic groups in the United States. But that advantage is concentrated in exactly the metros — San Francisco, San Jose, Seattle, and New York — where affordability remains most strained.

For younger Indian Americans and recent H-1B workers building toward homeownership, the numbers underscore a persistent tension: high incomes in tech hubs are often offset by even higher housing costs. First-time buyers in these markets face median home prices that can exceed $1 million.

What's Next

Redfin economists said affordability could improve slightly by year's end, but warned it could also worsen if interest rates rise more than expected, oil prices increase further, or inflation accelerates. The housing market has become a buyer's market in much of the country, giving shoppers more options and negotiating power, according to Xu. But for many prospective first-time buyers, the math still doesn't work.
